Wickard and Perez permit assessment of class effects without treating this individual's conduct as independently substantial. The position preserves judicial review, the need for a substantial class relationship and reasonable means, and the absence of a universal formal-findings prerequisite. It does not confer commerce power merely because safe schools are desirable or because this object once crossed a state line. It would reverse the constitutional dismissal and remand for the unresolved sentencing objections, rather than validate the entire conviction and sentence without further review.

+

+
+**Stevens.** His Dalm dissent directly supports taking the broad wrongfully-collected language and the pay-first structure seriously, while his California join preserves the distinction between a congressional remedy and a newly invented common-law one. Here the claim is timely and invokes express monetary consent. The strongest opposing route is Dalm's requirement to read §1346 with §§6511 and 7422, treating their taxpayer language as a claimant limitation. He accepts the integrated reading but rejects its proposed result: a person from whom the Government obtains the payment by asserting liens on property she claims is her own has a refund claim concerning that collection, and §6511's timing language does not silently remove the waiver for that claim. This does not rest on the nonbinding portion of his Dalm dissent or excuse late claims. Stahmann strengthens the conclusion that payment to free property is not an unsolicited gift, with its distinct statutory incidence acknowledged. He would refuse a supposed holding that all lien issues were conceded or that anyone may pay another's tax and demand a refund. His join requires separating jurisdiction from liability, preserving §7422(b)'s absence of a universal duress condition, and leaving the amount and merits to further proceedings.
+
+**O'Connor.** Her Dalm and Nordic Village joins require an enacted waiver read with its conditions; her California opinion rejects judicial creation of a refund right while leaving express remedies available. Those principles permit this suit because §1346 expressly addresses wrongful collection, not only erroneous assessment, and Williams presents her own payment extracted through asserted liens against claimed property. The strongest barrier is that she is not Rabin's taxpayer and §6511 says a claim is filed “by the taxpayer.” For these connected refund provisions, a person subjected to collection in this manner can make the timely claim concerning the amount obtained from her; absence of personal liability for the assessment does not place that collection beyond the explicit waiver. She would not define every payer as a taxpayer for every Code purpose. The separate third-party mechanisms have real prerequisites: no levy here and no agreed substitute fund. Their existence supplies no unstated exhaustion or exclusive-remedy command. Her support does not depend on whether Williams was told of those alternatives. She would refuse reasoning that relaxes sovereign immunity for hardship alone, treats the Secretary's permission as an obligation, or finds the liens invalid on the jurisdiction record. Affirmance authorizes adjudication, not payment.
+
+**Scalia.** His authorship of the actual Nordic Village opinion and his Dalm join make the connected text decisive. This waiver explicitly permits an action for a sum allegedly wrongfully collected under the revenue laws; unlike old §106(c), its monetary character cannot be avoided by a plausible nonmonetary reading. The strongest contrary construction treats §6511's “by the taxpayer” as a categorical restriction to the personally liable debtor. He reads that provision in the refund scheme as setting the conditions and time for refund claims, not overriding §1346's express collection language for a person made to pay through a lien asserted against her own claimed property. This narrow category does not depend on legislative history or a general remedial presumption. No clause supplied makes §7426 exclusive of this action, and its levy/fund conditions cannot be assumed away. Stahmann's treatment of the payments as nonvoluntary is a useful analogy, but its incidence and collector posture prevent making it the waiver. His join requires that the statutory text do the work and that §7422(b) not be replaced by a universal coercion requirement. He would refuse an opinion based merely on fairness, an invented concession, or a claim that he abandons Nordic Village whenever a remedy would be useful. He affirms only jurisdiction, reserving volunteered payments and merits defenses.
+
+**Kennedy.** His Dalm opinion supplies the closest personal starting point: §1346's broad words must be read with the statutory conditions for a duly filed refund claim. His Nordic Village and California joins reinforce Congress's control over the remedy. The strongest affirmance route is the distinction between assessment and collection, coupled with Williams's own payment to remove a lien and the absence of a levy or guaranteed substitute-fund route. He accepts those facts and does not dismiss the payment as a gift. Nevertheless, §6511's instruction that the refund claim be filed by the taxpayer, read with §7701's person-subject-to-tax definition, does not clearly include a person whose premise is that she is not liable for the tax. A lien collection can be wrongful without converting the property's claimant into that taxpayer. The differentiated third-party statutes reinforce this boundary, including their different conditions and treatment of the underlying assessment. Dalm did not already decide this identity question; the current conclusion extends its integrated method, not its precise holding. Stahmann's imposed economic incidence and collector remedy keep it from settling this distinct waiver. He would reverse without finding that any alternative remedy was guaranteed or that Williams failed to exhaust it. He can join only a statutory dismissal that preserves the unresolved merits and admits the practical limitations of the alternatives. He would refuse a ruling that the lien was valid or that the asserted concession has no effect on any properly authorized claim.
+
+**Souter.** His Nordic Village and California joins support fidelity to the actual waiver, not a common-law refund action. Here there is express monetary consent for wrongful collection and a timely claim about money obtained from the claimant through liens on her claimed property. The strongest opposing route is the connected taxpayer language and the special protections and deadlines of §7426. He finds the integrated affirmance reading better: the refund statutes encompass this collection relationship without deeming every nonliable donor a taxpayer, and the specific third-party remedies govern the transactions they actually describe rather than silently removing a broader express refund route. He would not use general jurisdiction alone as a waiver or rely on Stahmann without acknowledging its different statute. His join requires an explicit answer to §6511 and §7701, no categorical rule that taxpayer terminology is irrelevant, and no implication that §7426(c)'s assessment presumption disappears in an action brought under §7426. Its transfer to this different action is not decided. He would refuse an adjudication of the lien merits under the guise of standing. The lower-court remand remains necessary to determine what, if anything, is refundable.
+
+**Thomas.** His joins in Nordic Village and California provide his pertinent personal record: affirmative monetary relief and its conditions must come from Congress. The strongest opposing reading rests on the undeniably broad collection language and the reality that Williams paid to remove Government restraints from claimed property. He accepts that §1346 is a monetary waiver, but concludes its scope remains tied to the duly filed taxpayer claim prescribed by §§7422 and 6511. Section 7701's definition does not clearly turn an admittedly nonliable property claimant into the taxpayer merely because collection was attempted. This is a scope conclusion, not denial that collection can be illegal or that statutory waivers can be broadly worded. The distinct levy and substitute-fund routes indicate a separately designed third-party scheme without proving either route was actually open to Williams. Stahmann's different tax incidence and collector action do not remove this limitation. He would join Kennedy's integrated statutory ground at that scope, but would refuse any suggestion that a discretionary fund discharge was compulsory, that knowledge or failure to use an alternative independently defeats jurisdiction, or that all collections from another's property are lawful. He supports jurisdictional dismissal only; hardship does not itself enlarge consent, and no merits ruling follows.
+
+**Ginsburg.** No directly pertinent personal Williams-rule writing is established by this bounded packet. Her commitment is a legal application of the released statutes and actual precedents, not an attributed preexisting tax-refund view. The express waiver reaches a collection-based claim, and the connected refund provisions can give effect to that grant by treating the person subjected to this lien-backed collection as eligible to present the timely refund claim concerning her payment. The strongest contrary path applies the defined taxpayer term only to the legally liable person and emphasizes the specialized third-party remedies. She rejects making that limitation implicit in timing language when it would exclude the very alleged wrongful collection of this person's money; the narrow holding still requires the due administrative claim and says nothing about every volunteer. The specific remedies do not cover this record automatically: a lien is not a levy, a quiet-title action is not a refund, and a permitted substitute-fund agreement is not an actual agreement. Stahmann supports the distinction from a volunteered payment while its separate grounds remain visible. She would refuse any rationale that treats remedial inconvenience as an independent waiver or converts allegation of wrongful collection into proof. Her join requires a clear jurisdiction-only disposition and further proceedings for the disputed concession, lien grounds, and amount as necessary.
+
+**Breyer.** No directly pertinent personal Williams-rule writing is established; this is a bounded interpretation, not a claim about his prior position. The integrated scheme expressly offers monetary recovery for wrongful collection, and Williams used the claim process after payment exacted by a lien on her claimed property. The strongest reverse route reads “taxpayer” as a firm personal-liability limit, reinforced by carefully limited third-party remedies. He concludes that the collection language, the administrative claim provision, and the timing provision fit together without that exclusion: the person whose claimed property is used to obtain the payment can seek review of her collection claim while ordinary filing conditions remain intact. The absence of a levy and of an agreed fund confirms that recognizing this textual route does not simply rename an existing §7426 action, but availability of a convenient remedy is not the source of jurisdiction. He would not infer that Congress guaranteed a substitute-fund discharge or that every alternative had to be exhausted. His join requires preserving Nordic Village's clarity requirement, Dalm's actual timing rule, and California's refusal to manufacture a common-law claim. Stahmann is corroborative, not a substitute for the waiver. He affirms jurisdiction only and would refuse to set a refund amount or decide the contested merits on this record.
+
+### Scope, remedies, and unresolved questions
+
+The six affirming associate commitments support an express statutory route for this person's alleged wrongful collection through liens asserted against property she claims as her own, followed by a timely administrative refund claim. They do not create a general volunteer-payment action or make formal duress a universal prerequisite contrary to §7422(b). They do not waive the administrative claim requirement, decide every consequence of the word taxpayer elsewhere in the Code, or hold that inadequacy of another remedy independently confers jurisdiction.
+
+The two reversing associate commitments rest on the integrated claimant limitation and scope of consent. They do not rest on a failure to seek a substitute fund, assume a levy, or find that practical alternative relief was assured. Their proposed remedy is dismissal of this refund action for lack of jurisdiction, not a merits judgment approving the liens or foreclosing a different statutorily authorized action.
+
+Every associate reserves the merits of the refund, lien validity and priority, the effect and exact scope of any binding Government concession, payment components, and amount. The affirmative jurisdiction route leaves those matters for the lower court as necessary; the negative route does not reach them. No independent constitutional claim, universal right to contest the former husband's assessment, or broad equitable remedy is admitted or decided. The record's factual conflicts therefore do not block this threshold commitment. A later proposed merits award would require resolution of those conflicts and its own legal basis.

+## 49. Stone v. INS
+
+### Components and legal alternatives
+
+The reviewable question concerns the Sixth Circuit's dismissal of review of the July 26, 1991 original deportation order. The August 1991 motion preceded judicial review and sought reconsideration rather than reopening on new facts; the BIA denied it February 3, 1993. The March 25, 1993 judicial petition was within ninety days of that denial but outside ninety days of the original order. The lower court's separate denial of relief from the reconsideration refusal is a second judgment component, not an adjudication of original-order timeliness. Sources: 13 F.3d at 935–936, 938–939; validated packet, “Judgment, record, and scope.”
+
+**Path preserving original-order review:** Former §1105a(a) incorporates chapter 158 review, including its established reconsideration treatment unless an INA modification displaces it. Locomotive Engineers, 482 U.S. at 284–285, distinguishes exhaustion from a timely motion's actual effect on finality even under language declaring an agency order final when served. Ibarra supplies the related administrable finality principle without controlling this different statute. Section (a)(6)'s consolidation command still has work where judicial review precedes the reconsideration motion or where a later motion does not suspend the original deadline. On this path, a timely pre-review motion postpones review finality; the full ninety-day period begins upon disposition, and the original-order dismissal is reversed and remanded. A late motion does not resurrect an expired review period.
+
+The strongest objection is the amendment's explicit expectation of two judicial reviews, considered with the shortened period. This is a serious statutory argument. It does not, however, make consolidation text meaningless under the preserving construction: the provision can coordinate a previously filed original-order petition and a later petition concerning reconsideration. The objection must therefore be resolved by interpreting the INA modification, not by saying the competing construction is linguistically impossible.
+
+**Path requiring separate deadlines:** Section (a)(6) is a specific modification of the incorporated review procedure. Its command to consolidate review of the original order with separately sought review concerning reconsideration contemplates continuing finality of the first order. The amended short deadline and the two-order structure support a petition directed to each order within its own period. On this path the original-order dismissal is affirmed; neither an optional motion nor its denial starts a new period for the original order.
+
+The strongest objection is that the same consolidation command can operate without displacing the ordinary timely-motion rule. Locomotive Engineers is especially weighty because it concerns the very incorporated review chapter, not just criminal appeals. The separate-deadline construction must rest on the specific amendment's structural instruction; the regulations' execution and no-stay provisions, concern about delay, or a general preference for strict jurisdictional rules cannot alone answer the objection.

+## 49. Stone v. INS
+
+### Historical comparison and additional review
+
+History affirmed the original-order timeliness dismissal. Its associate support was Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas and Ginsburg; O'Connor, Souter and Breyer supported reversal. Kennedy's historical authorship and Breyer's historical dissent authorship are documentary facts only. The provisional model agreed with six of those eight judgment positions but placed Stevens and Ginsburg with the original-order-review supporters.
+
+The dispute turns on former §1105a(a)'s incorporation of chapter 158 **subject to its specified modifications**, particularly the 1990 command in (a)(6) to consolidate separately sought review of the original order and reconsideration. Locomotive Engineers, 482 U.S. at 279–285, supplies the ordinary rule that a timely administrative reconsideration motion postpones finality for judicial review; it also distinguishes the original order from a refusal to reopen for material error. Actual Ibarra supplies the analogous timely criminal reconsideration rule, and actual Darby forbids extra exhaustion requirements in the specified APA setting. Neither holds that Congress cannot alter the ordinary rule in an express agency-specific review scheme.
+
+The incorporation argument remains a lawful and substantial alternative. Consolidation can have work when judicial review begins before agency reconsideration; mandatory consolidation differs from an ordinary discretionary ability to manage related reviews. But that argument requires choosing how the INA's specific exception coordinates two independently pursued review objects. It does not establish that the no-tolling construction contradicts Locomotive Engineers. Conversely, the separate-finality position cannot accurately say that consolidation has literally no conceivable application under the competing construction. Its sufficient ground is that the structure of the **amended** review statute calls for original-order review within its own period while separately permitting later review of reconsideration, with mandatory consolidation when both are before the court. The shortening of the original period corroborates that construction; no-stay regulations and delay policy alone do not establish it.
+
+Additional review of Stevens's entire Locomotive Engineers writing matters. His objection there concerned a judicially created exclusion from review of material-error reopening denials where the enacted text did not make that distinction, 482 U.S. at 287–295. He recognized that restrictive review language can control and distinguished statutory settings containing it, id. at 292 n.7. That is not a commitment that an express modification in another statute must leave the ordinary finality rule untouched. His actual Ibarra and Darby joins preserve ordinary rules in their own domains. His public Gustafson join accepts the relevance of statutory context. Together those sources support a serious incorporation argument, but supply no changed premise that would explain rejecting this particular INA construction when his historical position accepted it.

+For Ginsburg, the provisional reliance on her public Gustafson dissent identifies a method, not a new rule about incorporation or finality. Her insistence that section 10 should not erase an express section 2 definition leaves contextual qualification available when the enacted provisions warrant it. Former §1105a(a) expressly introduces its enumerated exceptions; treating (a)(6) as a modification does not disregard an unqualified incorporation. She was not a member of the Ibarra or Darby Courts, and no personal join in them is attributed. +### Competing legal paths and precedent treatment
+
+**Textual exclusion with express precedent treatment.** A federal court is not an enumerated executive department or, in the relevant statutory usage, an agency of the United States. The broad words “any matter” and “jurisdiction” describe the functions of an included entity; they do not independently establish which entities are included. Section 6's context qualification is genuine, but general antifraud purpose and the absence of a demonstrated narrowing intent in 1934 do not establish that every branch is a department under the enacted formulation. The separate agency words likewise cannot be read to make every body exercising governmental authority an agency without regard to their setting. On this path, Bramblett's all-branch construction must be rejected expressly, including its reasoning supporting legislative-branch coverage; the objection cannot be evaded merely by calling the judicial passage dictum. The present judgment decides courts and these filings, not the outcome of an unpresented prosecution involving another institution on an independently established agency theory.
+
+The strongest objection is statutory stare decisis: Bramblett considered the same proviso, settled its meaning, was later used in Rodgers, and may be revised by Congress. The exclusion path requires more than repeating disagreement. Its sufficient justification is the combined defect of displacing the express default with general predecessor-purpose reasoning, the resulting need to improvise unstable function-based criminal boundaries, and the absence here of contract, property, or institutional-benefit arrangements comparable to Hilton and Allied-Bruce that depend on the broader coverage. Prosecution expectations are relevant but do not by themselves cure a materially overextended definition of a crime. Rodgers's jurisdiction holding survives for an actual department or agency; its footnote 4 reserved rather than decided the judicial-function issue. No generalized right to make false statements follows.
+
+**Retain Bramblett and reject a judicial-function exception.** The §6 proviso expressly allows branch-wide meaning, Bramblett exercised that contextual judgment after examining this statute's development, and the subsequent statutory system supplies no sufficiently concrete reason to overrule it. Once that construction is retained, excluding judicial functions from “any matter” lacks an enacted basis. Rodgers supports authorized-function coverage and ordinary knowledge/materiality protections while expressly leaving the exception open. Heintz supplies a current, bounded analogy against an invented litigation exemption; it does not itself construe this criminal statute. Factual lies in these pleadings are not treated as innocent legal argument or a not-guilty plea. The Government's asset-collection characterization is unnecessary to this path, not a lower-court finding.
+
+The strongest objection is that the ordinary definition excludes courts and overlapping perjury/obstruction provisions protect judicial proceedings with deliberately different limits. The retention path answers that Congress wrote a context proviso and that Bramblett resolved it; statutory overlap does not itself exclude unsworn factual lies. Lenity does not undo a meaning these Justices regard as settled. This path supplies no universal knowledge-of-illegality rule, approval of every prosecution of litigation conduct, or retroactive penalty increase.
+
+**Intermediate exception or private-litigation path.** The circuit tradition and Nelson's dissent provide a serious narrower alternative. The court's adjudicative machinery differs from administrative/housekeeping acts; a private trustee is not automatically the United States as litigant. Against it stand the absence of a textual exception, inconsistent boundaries, and the fact that the actual counts charge factual assertions rather than merely testing legal sufficiency. On either intermediate theory, classification must be performed expressly. The lower court did not reach the Government's administrative-asset-collection alternative. A remand to address that preserved issue would be distinct from a direction to vacate the counts. None of the eight selects this intermediate path as a sufficient ground on the present provisional record; the individual barriers below explain why. No finding that the claims were harmless, truthful, sworn, or incapable of affecting estate administration is invented.
